Acute angle-closure glaucoma is top-ranked due to classic triad of severe ocular pain, blurred vision, and inability to open the eye—often accompanied by conjunctival injection, corneal edema, and mid-dilated nonreactive pupil; it is vision-threatening within hours. Bacterial keratitis follows closely: rapid progression, intense pain, and decreased vision are hallmark, especially with risk factors like contact lens wear or trauma (not yet elicited but common). HSV keratitis is highly plausible given acute painful blur, dendritic ulcers may not yet be visible on casual exam, and recurrence can present aggressively. Anterior uveitis (especially acute HLA-B27-related) fits well—painful, blurry, photophobic—but typically less severe pain than angle closure or infectious keratitis, and often with cells/flare on slit lamp. Corneal foreign body is included as a common, treatable cause of acute unilateral pain and blur; though often associated with trauma history, it may be forgotten or asymptomatic initially before inflammation escalates. Less likely diagnoses (e.g., optic neuritis, retinal detachment, migraine) were excluded due to absence of relative afferent pupillary defect, lack of visual field loss description, absence of headache/neurologic symptoms, and presence of severe pain—which is atypical for posterior segment or neuro-ophthalmic causes."}
